Soil respiration is the release of carbon dioxide (CO₂) from soil, mostly by microorganisms that break down organic matter. Students investigated how temperature, moisture, and the supply of organic carbon affect the rate of soil respiration.

In each trial, a 200 g core of soil collected from a single meadow was placed in a sealed 1 L glass jar. After 24 hours, the CO₂ concentration in the air inside the jar was measured with an infrared gas analyzer and converted to a CO₂ flux, in milligrams of CO₂ per kilogram of soil per hour (mg/kg/h).

Study 1
Four cores were adjusted to a moisture content of 25% by mass and incubated at 5 °C, 15 °C, 25 °C, or 35 °C (Trials 1-4, Table 1).

Study 2
Five cores were incubated at 25 °C after being adjusted to a moisture content of 5%, 15%, 25%, 35%, or 45% by mass (Trials 5-9).

Study 3
Four cores were adjusted to 25% moisture and incubated at 25 °C. Before incubation, 1.0 g of glucose dissolved in 5 mL of water was mixed into two of the cores; 5 mL of water alone was mixed into the other two. One core from each pair was first autoclaved (heated under pressure to 121 °C for 30 min) and allowed to cool before anything was mixed in (Trials 10-13).

options.C: the soil cores had the same moisture content as in Study 1.

A capacitor stores electric charge. When a charged capacitor is connected across a resistor, charge flows through the resistor and the voltage across the capacitor decreases over time. Students studied how the rate of this decrease depends on the resistance R, the capacitance C, and the initial voltage V₀.

In each trial, a capacitor was charged to V₀ with a power supply, then disconnected from the supply and connected across a resistor at time t = 0. A data logger recorded the capacitor voltage every 0.1 s. The discharge time, t_d, was defined as the time at which the voltage had fallen to 37% of V₀. Each trial was repeated three times, and the average t_d was recorded.

Study 1
A 470 μF capacitor was charged to V₀ = 9.0 V and discharged through a resistor of 10 kΩ, 22 kΩ, 47 kΩ, or 100 kΩ (Figure 1).

Study 2
A 47 kΩ resistor was used with a 100 μF, 220 μF, 470 μF, or 1,000 μF capacitor, each charged to V₀ = 9.0 V (Figure 1).

Study 3
The 470 μF capacitor was discharged through the 47 kΩ resistor after being charged to V₀ = 3.0 V, 6.0 V, 9.0 V, or 12.0 V. The values of t_d were 22.2 s, 22.0 s, 22.3 s, and 22.1 s, respectively.

Enzymes are proteins that speed up chemical reactions. Heating an enzyme can increase the rate of the reaction it catalyzes, but heat can also unfold the protein and permanently destroy its activity. Researchers studied the effect of temperature on an esterase, an enzyme isolated from a soil fungus that converts a colorless ester into a yellow product.

In each trial, 2.0 mL of buffer solution (pH 7.0) containing 0.10 mg of the enzyme was placed in a water bath at a set temperature. After a pre-incubation period at that temperature, 0.10 mL of ester solution was added, and the increase in yellow color over the next 60 s was measured with a spectrophotometer. From this measurement, the initial reaction rate, in micromoles of product per minute (μmol/min), was calculated.

Study 1
The pre-incubation period was 1 min. Trials were conducted at 20 °C, 30 °C, 40 °C, 50 °C, 60 °C, and 70 °C (Figure 1).

Study 2
The procedure of Study 1 was repeated, except that the pre-incubation period was 30 min (Figure 1).

Study 3
The procedure of Study 2 was repeated, except that the buffer solution also contained 20% glycerol by volume, a compound thought to stabilize protein structure (Figure 1).

The ring orbits 1.6 planetary radii from the planet's center, inside the distance at which tidal forces prevent loose material from gathering into a moon. Its particles are more than 90% water ice by mass, its total mass is about 10^16 kg, and two small moons orbit just inside and just outside its edges. Two scientists discuss how the ring formed.

Scientist 1

The ring is young, no more than 10 million years old. A small icy moon drifted inside the tidal limit and was torn apart; the two moons at the ring's edges are its largest surviving pieces, and they keep the ring narrow. Fresh debris is bright, nearly pure ice, and it darkens as meteoroid dust settles on it at a known rate. The probe measured the ring's reflectivity at 0.6, comparable to fresh frost, whereas the planet's oldest icy moons reflect less than 0.3. At the known dust rate, a surface that bright cannot have been exposed for more than a few tens of millions of years.

The ring is primordial: material left over from the planet's formation 4.5 billion years ago that never gathered into a moon because it lies inside the tidal limit. The edge moons formed at the same time and have confined the ring ever since, so its narrowness says nothing about its age. Neither does its brightness. Ring particles collide constantly, and each collision chips off the darkened outer layer and exposes clean ice, so a continually resurfaced ring stays bright indefinitely. For six summers, residents of a farming valley have suffered an illness marked by fever, joint pain, and rash. Cases occur only from July through September; nearly all patients live within 2 km of the valley's river; a previously unknown virus can be isolated from patients' blood; and the same virus is present in the blood of the valley's cattle, which show no signs of disease. Three scientists propose how the virus reaches people.

Scientist 1

The virus is carried by biting midges that breed in flooded irrigation ditches along the river. Midges feed on cattle and on people at dusk, and the virus multiplies in a midge for several days. Cases should be fewest in years when the ditches are drained early, and people who spend evenings outdoors should be at greatest risk. Traps set within 500 m of the ditches collected 20 times as many midges as traps set 2 km away, and pooled midges from the ditch-side traps contained the virus.

Scientist 2

The virus is carried by ticks that feed on cattle. A tick picks up the virus from a cow and passes it to a person who handles cattle or walks through pasture. The late-summer timing of cases matches the activity peak of the tick's adult stage. Cases should concentrate in households that keep cattle, whatever their water source. Of the patients' households, 80% keep cattle within 100 m of the house, and ticks removed from those cattle carried the virus.

Scientist 3

No animal carries the virus. Infected cattle shed the virus in urine, which is washed into the river and into shallow household wells when fields are irrigated in summer. People are infected by drinking or bathing in that water. Households supplied with piped water from outside the valley should have few cases, however many cattle they keep. Virus genetic material was detected in 12 of 30 shallow wells sampled in August but in none of the same wells in March.

Surveys have established that the bedrock is limestone lying beneath 2 to 4 m of glacial till deposited about 15,000 years ago; that the depressions form chains aligned northeast-southwest; that each has a flat floor of fine silt; and that permafrost was present in the region until about 12,000 years ago but is absent today. The depressions are sinkholes. Groundwater moving along fractures in the limestone dissolves the rock and opens cavities; when a cavity grows large enough, the till above it collapses into it. Because dissolution continues today, new depressions should keep appearing, and each depression should be underlain by broken rock. A borehole drilled at the center of one depression passed through 3 m of silt and then 4 m of limestone rubble before reaching solid rock, and aerial photographs show two depressions that were absent 40 years ago.

Three years after an office building opened, its tempered glass facade panels began cracking without being struck; within two years, 14 of 900 panels broke. Because tempered glass shatters completely, fracture origins were inferred from fragments left in the frame. Two students propose causes.

Student 1

The panels contain nickel sulfide inclusions, tiny stones formed in molten glass. Tempering freezes each stone in a high-temperature form; over several years it converts to a low-temperature form about 4% larger, and a stone in the panel's tensile core that expands this much cracks the glass. Warmth speeds the conversion, which is why the sunlit faces failed first. A stone that has nearly finished converting can be pushed over the threshold by any small added stress, including morning warming, so the hour of a break says little about its cause. Fragments from three failed panels showed a butterfly-shaped fracture origin near the panel's center around a dark particle, and 2 of 50 unbroken panels from the batch shattered when heated uniformly in an oven.

Student 2

The failures are thermal. Morning sun heats the exposed part of a panel while the fin-shaded strip and frame-covered edge stay cool; the hot center expands and pulls the cool edge into tension. Tempered glass resists this unless an edge was chipped during installation; the chip concentrates stress. Fracture origins should therefore lie at the edge nearest the fin's shadow, failures should peak in the morning, when the difference is greatest, and removing the fins should end the failures. Only sunlit faces experience such differences, which is why the north and east faces have no failures.
